summary: Describes how to prepare internationalized domain name labels so that input and comparison work sensibly for users everywhere. It is a profile of stringprep and is part of the set of protocols for internationalizing DNS. It was replaced by RFC 5891.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC says how to tidy up a domain name label written in a non-English script before it is stored or compared. It picks one set of characters, one set of character substitutions, one normalization form and a list of forbidden outputs, so two spellings of the same name end up identical.

questions: what does nameprep do in idna
which unicode version does nameprep use
subtitle: The rulebook for cleaning up internationalized domain name labels so look-alike inputs compare as equal.

tldr.problem: People type internationalized domain names in many ways, and the same name written by two people can differ in case, in form, or in characters that look identical on screen. Two systems that compare such names literally would disagree about whether they are the same name.
tldr.mechanism: Nameprep is a profile of stringprep that fixes the character repertoire, the mappings, the Unicode normalization form, the prohibited output and the bidirectional checks to apply to each domain name label before it is stored or compared.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3491 was a Proposed Standard and it has been obsoleted by RFC 5891.

facts.label: Applies to
facts.value: Domain name labels, not whole domain names

sections.title: What Nameprep Is For
sections.content:
The RFC describes how to prepare internationalized domain name labels so that name input and name comparison work in ways that make sense for typical users throughout the world. It is a profile of the stringprep protocol, used as part of a suite of on-the-wire protocols for internationalizing the Domain Name System.

The processing rules are intended only for internationalized domain names, not for arbitrary text. The profile fixes the things stringprep requires: the intended applicability of the profile, which is internationalized domain names processed by IDNA; the character repertoire that is the input and output to stringprep, which is Unicode 3.2; the mappings used; the Unicode normalization used; the characters prohibited as output; and the handling of bidirectional characters.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules apply to one job only: making a domain name label written in a non-English script behave predictably. They are not a general-purpose text cleaner.

sections.title: How Nameprep Fits with IDNA and Stringprep
sections.content:
Nameprep is used by the IDNA protocol for preparing domain names. It is not designed for any other purpose, and it is explicitly not designed for processing arbitrary free text and should not be used for that purpose. Implementations of Nameprep must fully implement Stringprep.

Nameprep is used to process domain name labels, not domain names. IDNA calls nameprep for each label in a domain name, not for the whole domain name.

The RFC marks one point as important: this profile must be used with the IDNA protocol, because the IDNA protocol has additional prohibitions that are checked outside of this profile. So nameprep does the label-level work, and IDNA applies its own extra rules on top.
sections.plainLanguage: Nameprep is one step inside a larger scheme. It cleans up each label of a domain name separately, and the scheme that uses it applies further checks of its own.

sections.title: Character Repertoire and Mapping
sections.content:
The profile uses Unicode 3.2, as defined in the stringprep specification's Appendix A. Unicode 3.2 is the set of characters that can go in and come out of the processing; anything outside it is out of scope for these rules.

The profile specifies mapping using table B.1 and table B.2 from stringprep. These are the tables that say which characters are mapped to other characters, and which are left alone. Mapping is the first of the steps, and everything after it operates on the mapped result.

The set of mappings is the same for every domain name in the profile, so two different domains are compared after the same substitutions have been applied to both.
sections.plainLanguage: Only characters from one version of Unicode are allowed, and a fixed table says which of them get rewritten to another character before anything else happens.

sections.title: Normalization, Prohibited Output and Bidirectional Text
sections.content:
The profile specifies using Unicode normalization form KC, as described in stringprep. Normalization puts a string into one canonical form so that two spellings that differ only in how the same characters are combined end up byte-for-byte identical.

The profile specifies prohibiting the following stringprep tables as output: C.1.2, C.2.2, C.3, C.4, C.5, C.6, C.7, C.8 and C.9. These are the characters that must not survive into the prepared string, because they have no place in a domain name label or would let two different labels look the same.

The profile also specifies checking bidirectional strings as described in section 6 of stringprep. This is the check that keeps text written right to left, such as Arabic or Hebrew, in a well-formed shape after mapping and normalization have run.

Finally, the RFC addresses unassigned code points. If the processing in IDNA specifies that a list of unassigned code points be used, the system uses table A.1 from stringprep as its list of unassigned code points.
sections.plainLanguage: After the substitutions, the string is put into one standard form, checked against a list of characters that must not appear, and checked for right-to-left text. Code points that Unicode has not assigned are handled from a fixed table.

sections.title: Registration of the Profile
sections.content: The RFC records that this is a profile of stringprep and that it has been registered by IANA in the stringprep profile registry. The registration names the profile Nameprep, identifies the RFC in which the profile is defined as the document itself, and records that this is the first version of Nameprep.
sections.plainLanguage: The profile has a name in the IANA registry, and the registry records that this document is the first version of it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC starts from a fact about Unicode and ISO/IEC 10646: they contain many characters that look similar. Because it is impossible to map similar-looking characters without a great deal of context, such as knowing the fonts used, stringprep does nothing to map similar-looking characters together, nor does it prohibit some characters because they look like others.

Security on the Internet partly relies on the DNS, so any change to the characteristics of the DNS can change the security of much of the Internet. Domain names are used by users to connect to Internet servers, and the security of the Internet would be compromised if a user entering a single internationalized name could be connected to different servers based on different interpretations of that name.

The RFC also warns about scale and about old assumptions. This document vastly increases the number of characters available in domain names. Every program that uses special characters in conjunction with domain names may be vulnerable to attack based on the new characters allowed by this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Two different scripts can contain characters that look identical on screen, and this RFC cannot tell them apart. So a name that looks the same to a person may not be the same name to a resolver, which is a risk for anyone comparing them by eye.

viz.caption: THE PROFILE PARAMETERS, ILLUSTRATIVE AND NOT A VERBATIM QUOTE

data.title: What the Nameprep profile fixes
data.code:
character repertoire : Unicode 3.2
mapping             : stringprep tables B.1, B.2
normalization       : Unicode form KC
prohibited output   : stringprep tables C.1.2, C.2.2,
                      C.3, C.4, C.5, C.6, C.7, C.8, C.9
bidirectional check : stringprep section 6
unassigned code pts : stringprep table A.1
